clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in SLC5A2, encoding the sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT2 in the proximal tubule
The hallmark is persistent glucosuria with normal blood glucose and a normal oral glucose tolerance test
It is a benign, usually asymptomatic condition discovered incidentally on urinalysis, not a form of diabetes mellitus
Inheritance shows co-dominant expression: heterozygotes have mild glucosuria while homozygotes or compound heterozygotes lose larger quantities
Rarely, heavy glucose loss is associated with polyuria, mild volume depletion, or enuresis, and occasionally episodic ketosis during fasting or pregnancy
No specific treatment is needed; reassurance and confirmation that carbohydrate metabolism is normal are the mainstays
The transporter is the pharmacological target of SGLT2-inhibitor drugs, which reproduce a similar glucosuric state therapeutically
reference.pathophysiology: SGLT2 is a high-capacity, low-affinity sodium-glucose cotransporter on the apical membrane of the early proximal tubule and is responsible for reabsorbing the bulk of filtered glucose. Loss-of-function variants in SLC5A2 lower the renal threshold for glucose, so glucose appears in the urine at normal plasma concentrations. Because systemic glucose handling and insulin secretion are intact, blood glucose remains normal and there is no hyperglycaemia. The degree of glucosuria reflects the residual transporter activity, with homozygous defects producing the largest urinary losses. Downstream SGLT1 in the later proximal tubule reclaims some glucose, limiting total loss and generally keeping the condition clinically silent.
additionalDifferentials: Glucose-galactose malabsorption (SGLT1 defect, presenting with diarrhoea)
additionalInvestigations: Simultaneous blood glucose and urine glucose showing glucosuria with normoglycaemia
Oral glucose tolerance test to exclude diabetes
Urinalysis for other proximal tubular markers to exclude Fanconi syndrome
Quantification of daily urinary glucose loss where clinically relevant
SLC5A2 gene sequencing when confirmation is desired
redFlags: Coexisting aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, or proteinuria suggesting Fanconi syndrome rather than isolated glucosuria
Symptomatic volume depletion or dehydration from heavy glucose loss
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign with a normal life expectancy and does not progress to renal impairment; most people remain asymptomatic and require no treatment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the glucosuria as diabetes mellitus and starting unnecessary treatment
Failing to distinguish isolated renal glucosuria from generalised Fanconi syndrome
Not counselling about occasional fasting ketosis or dehydration in heavy losers
references: OMIM entry for familial renal glucosuria
management: Reassure that this is a benign condition with normal carbohydrate metabolism rather than diabetes mellitus, and that no specific treatment is required
Confirm normoglycaemia with a normal oral glucose tolerance test and HbA1c to exclude diabetes before labelling
Ensure adequate fluid and salt intake to offset any osmotic diuresis in heavy glucosuria
Monitor for and correct volume depletion or ketosis during fasting, intercurrent illness or pregnancy
Exclude generalised proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome) if other tubular markers are abnormal
Offer genetic counselling with SLC5A2 testing when confirmation is desired, noting co-dominant inheritance explains variable severity
